title: Why Do We Overthink Everything?
hook: It's late at night, and you're replaying one awkward sentence from this afternoon, again and again. Why does your brain do this?
notes: Curated sample for the psychology visual identity. Claims follow the research pack (Wikipedia: Rumination (psychology), Co-rumination). Coping ideas are presented as psychologists' suggestions (refocus on planning, positive distraction), not medical advice. No statistics are used.

beats.narration: It's late at night, and you're replaying one awkward sentence from this afternoon, again and again. Why does your brain do this?
We've all been there: a text that went unanswered, a choice that's already made, a conversation we just can't stop rewinding.
Psychologists have a name for this loop. And the surprising part? It feels like solving a problem, when it usually isn't.
It's called rumination: repetitively focusing on a problem, its causes and its consequences. Your thoughts circle the same track, over and over, without going anywhere new.
Researchers noticed that ruminators focus on their feelings about a problem, instead of on actions that could change it. So the loop keeps feeding itself.
And every what-if opens up more what-ifs. One small choice becomes a whole tree of possibilities, most of which will never happen.
Here's the twist: even talking it over can keep the loop spinning. One study found that stress hormones rise when friends dwell on problems together.
So what breaks the loop? Psychologists suggest shifting from why did this happen, to what can I do next, or switching to something genuinely absorbing.

items.text: Ask: what can I do next?

beats.narration: Overthinking feels like progress, but real progress starts with one small next step. Stay curious!
